The North Pole. The northernmost point of Earth's axis, located in the Arctic Ocean surrounded by pack ice. Unlike the South Pole's solid Antarctic continent, the North Pole sits on a drifting ice sheet with no permanent land, making it one of Earth's most extreme and inaccessible locations.

The North Pole is situated at ninety degrees north latitude in the Arctic Ocean, roughly four hundred fifty miles north of the nearest land in Greenland and the Canadian Arctic.

Unlike Antarctica, there is no permanent research station at the North Pole. Ice thickness varies from six to forty feet and constantly drifts with ocean currents.

Early polar explorers faced near-impossible odds. Frederick Cook claimed to reach it in nineteen oh-eight, followed by Robert Peary in nineteen oh-nine, though both claims remain disputed.

The North Pole experiences extreme seasons: continuous daylight in summer and continuous darkness in winter, making navigation extraordinarily challenging.

The USS Nautilus, the world's first nuclear submarine, made history in nineteen fifty-eight by passing under the Arctic ice, reaching the North Pole submerged.

The magnetic north pole, where compass needles point, differs from the geographic North Pole and has shifted significantly over geological time and historical records.

Arctic exploration in the twentieth century was driven by Cold War competition between the Soviet Union and the United States, with both nations exploring polar regions.
